prompt: What is the one difference between `v6-escaped.txt` and `v18-order.txt`?
hint: Read the `diff`.

choices.text: The categories are listed in the opposite order
choices.why: Right: one line, the same five labels backwards.

choices.text: `other` was added as a sixth category
choices.why: `other` was already in the list; it moved to the front.

choices.text: The message is no longer escaped
choices.why: Both still use `{{message|xml}}`.

choices.text: The urgencies are listed from high to low instead of low to high
choices.why: The urgency line is identical in both files.

prompt: Reversing the list of categories, how many of the seventy answers changed?
hint: The first line of `pl compare --answers`.

prompt: The reversed list moved `t37`, `h07`, `h15` and `h28`. What do those four messages have in common?
hint: Would a list order move a message about a double charge?

choices.text: They are the longest messages in the set
choices.why: Length is not what the order acts on.

choices.text: They are all about the label that moved to the front
choices.why: None of them is about `other`; that is why two became wrong.

choices.text: Little evidence for any one label, so a small push decides them
choices.why: Right: an order moves the close calls and leaves the clear messages alone.

choices.text: They come from the holdout set
choices.why: `t37` is a dev case.

prompt: `pl compare` without `--answers` reported `t04` as broken by the reversed list, but its category did not change. Why did it break?
hint: Look at the reply under `v18-order`.

choices.text: The urgency changed from high to normal
choices.why: The reply still says high.

choices.text: A sentence in front of the JSON, re-rolled by editing the prompt
choices.why: Right: the stand-in rolls its habits from the prompt's exact text, so any edit re-rolls them.

choices.text: The sign test marked it
choices.why: The sign test only summarises the cases that changed.

choices.text: The new list made `account` an invalid label for a case about logging in
choices.why: `account` is in both lists.

prompt: *Calibrate Before Use* (Zhao and others, 2021) named a recency bias. What did GPT-3 favour?
hint: Recency is about position in the prompt.

choices.text: The answer it gave on the previous call
choices.why: Each call is independent; the bias is inside one prompt.

choices.text: The most recent version of the prompt
choices.why: That is a question about versioning, not about bias.

choices.text: The newest training data
choices.why: The paper is about what is in the prompt.

choices.text: Labels of the last examples
choices.why: Right: where an example sits changes what the model answers.

prompt: Adding *Most messages we get are about delivery* moved eight answers. Where did they go?
hint: Read the right-hand side of each line.

choices.text: All eight to delivery
choices.why: Right: every change pointed the same way.

choices.text: Four to delivery and four away from it
choices.why: None moved away from delivery.

choices.text: Spread across the five categories, as noise would be
choices.why: That is what noise looks like; this was not noise.

choices.text: To `other`, the label the sentence left out
choices.why: That was the reversed list, in the section before.

prompt: Suppose it is true that most of the shop's messages are about delivery. Why is the sentence still a bad thing to put in the prompt?
hint: Who is the sentence about, and who does the model apply it to?

choices.text: It is false for the holdout set, whose messages were chosen to be harder
choices.why: The problem does not depend on whether it is true.

choices.text: It describes the whole inbox and is applied to each message
choices.why: Right: every message about something else starts behind.

choices.text: It makes the prompt too long
choices.why: One sentence; the cost is in the answers, not the tokens.

choices.text: Models ignore sentences in the first paragraph of a prompt, so it wastes tokens and does nothing
choices.why: It did plenty: eight answers moved.

prompt: Of the eight answers the leading sentence moved, how many had been right before it was added?
hint: Line the compare output up with the person's labels.

prompt: A sentence like *most messages are about delivery* states a base ___: a fact about the inbox, not about the message in front of the model.
hint: How often something happens across the whole population.

prompt: Which of these, found in a prompt, are worth testing as leading words? Choose all that apply.
hint: Anything that says what to expect.

choices.text: *Customers usually want a refund.*
choices.why: Yes: an expectation about the customer.

choices.text: *Nearly all messages are about billing.*
choices.why: Yes: a base rate.

choices.text: *For instance, a late parcel.*
choices.why: Yes: a sentence that names one kind of message is tested like the others.

choices.text: *Answer with only a JSON object.*
choices.why: That says what to do with every message, which is what a prompt is for.

prompt: `pl compare --answers` between the skewed and the balanced prompts listed 23 different answers. On how many did the skewed prompt say billing?
hint: Read the left-hand side of each line.

prompt: Every one of the 23 differences pointed the same way. Why does that matter more than the number 23?
hint: What would noise look like?

choices.text: Twenty-three is too few to mean anything
choices.why: Twenty-three of seventy is a lot, and the direction makes it clearer still.

choices.text: Noise scatters; one direction is a bias
choices.why: Right: a pull towards one label shows up as changes that all point at it.

choices.text: It shows the balanced prompt is right on all 23
choices.why: It changed them; the check says how many it got right.

choices.text: It means the format changed on those cases
choices.why: `--answers` reads leniently; format is not in it.

prompt: The category check went from 45 to 57. Why does that not measure the effect of the label count alone?
hint: What else differs between the two sets of examples?

choices.text: Format failures are mixed into the category count, as they were with the reversed list
choices.why: Both prompts parse on all seventy here.

choices.text: The balanced prompt is longer
choices.why: Both have five examples.

choices.text: The example messages differ too, and examples pull by likeness
choices.why: Right: it compares two sets of examples, which is the decision you face.

choices.text: The sign test was not run
choices.why: A p-value would not separate the two causes either.

prompt: Zhao and others proposed contextual calibration against majority label bias. What does it ask the model about?
hint: An input that carries no evidence for any label.

choices.text: A content-free input such as `N/A`
choices.why: Right: whatever it leans towards there is the prompt's own lean, which is then corrected.

choices.text: Its own confidence in each label
choices.why: Stated confidence is a different subject, and lesson 21 shows how far it can be trusted.

choices.text: The same message with the examples in every possible order
choices.why: That would measure order effects, at great cost; it is not the method.

choices.text: A person's label for every test case
choices.why: The point is that it needs no labels at all.

prompt: Why is one example per label not neutral either?
hint: What does an even set say about the inbox?

choices.text: Five examples cost too many tokens
choices.why: Cost is a separate question; this is about the answers.

choices.text: The stand-in ignores examples after the third, so the last two labels are never pulled
choices.why: Every example in the prompt adds its pull.

choices.text: It implies equal odds for all five
choices.why: Right: that is false for most inboxes, and either choice is a choice to make on purpose.

choices.text: A balanced set has no billing example
choices.why: It has one of each, billing included.

prompt: What does a counterfactual test change between its two copies of a message?
hint: Everything else stays byte for byte.

choices.text: The prompt
choices.why: The prompt is the same; that is what makes the comparison about the person.

choices.text: The attribute that must not matter, and nothing else
choices.why: Right: a name here, and only the name.

choices.text: The temperature, to see how stable the answers are
choices.why: That is a different test; this one keeps the settings fixed.

choices.text: The label a person gave
choices.why: The labels are identical in both files.

prompt: Maria's and John's eight messages got the same answers. What does that tell you about real models?
hint: What would the stand-in need in order to treat a name differently?

choices.text: That names do not affect them
choices.why: The test was run on the stand-in, not on a real model.

choices.text: That eight pairs are enough to be sure
choices.why: Eight is a demonstration, and these eight say nothing about a real model at all.

choices.text: That the test was badly built
choices.why: The test is sound; the stand-in just cannot fail it.

choices.text: Nothing, since no name is a keyword
choices.why: Right: a test that cannot fail tells you nothing about what it tests.

prompt: Under `names-b`, `n06` came back with a sentence in front of its JSON; under `names-a` it did not. What is that?
hint: Did the category or the urgency change?

choices.text: A bias against the name John
choices.why: A bias would move an answer in a direction; nothing about the answer moved.

choices.text: A formatting roll that depends on the exact text
choices.why: Right: noise that happens to depend on the name.

choices.text: A different urgency
choices.why: Both say normal.

choices.text: A sign the prompt is not delimited
choices.why: `v6-escaped` delimits the message.

prompt: On a real model, how would you find the noise floor for a counterfactual test?
hint: What differs between two runs that should be identical?

choices.text: Run the same file twice and compare the two runs
choices.why: Right: a difference between the names only counts above that.

choices.text: Use temperature 0, which makes the floor zero on every model
choices.why: It is zero in the stand-in; on a real model it is not guaranteed.

choices.text: Count the format failures
choices.why: Format is one source of noise; the floor is about answers.

choices.text: Compare `names-a` with `names-b`
choices.why: That is the test itself; the floor is what you compare it against.

prompt: Put the four tests of this lesson in order of how many answers moved, fewest first.
items: A sentence saying most messages are about delivery
Four billing examples instead of one per label

prompt: Match each source of bias to the stand-in's declared rule for it.
hint: Each is a constant or rule in `standin.py`.

pairs.left: A sentence about what most messages are

pairs.right: No rule: it is not a keyword

prompt: A colleague adds *Customers usually write about returns* and the category check goes up by one. What do you look at before keeping it?
hint: A count of passes mixes several things.

choices.text: Nothing more: the score went up
choices.why: One case can move for reasons unrelated to the change, and a gain can hide losses.

choices.text: Whether the summaries got longer
choices.why: The sentence acts on the category, so that is where to look.

choices.text: The answers with and without it: which moved, and whether all of them moved to returns
choices.why: Right: `pl compare --answers`, then the person's labels for what moved.

choices.text: The same run at a higher temperature
choices.why: That adds noise without answering the question.
